textClass.keywords: Instrumental variable estimation Peer effects Sieve estimation Social interactions Spatial autoregressive models

div.p: In this study, we consider cross-sectional interaction models including spatial autoregressive models and peer effects models as special cases. Our model allows the endogenous effect -the effect of others' outcomes on one's own outcome -to be nonlinear and nonparametric. For the model estimation, we propose a sieve instrumental variable estimator and establish both its consistency and asymptotic normality. Furthermore, we propose a nonparametric specification test for the linearity of the endogenous effect. Under the null hypothesis of linearity, we show that the test statistic is asymptotically distributed as normal. As an empirical illustration, we focus on the data on regional economic performance investigated by Gennaioli et al. (2013). This empirical analysis highlights the usefulness of the proposed model and method.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Cross-sectional interdependence among units is an essential factor in the analysis of spatial data and peer effects. In particular, precisely estimating the endogenous effect -the effect of others' outcomes on one's own outcome -is important from a policy perspective. The existence of the endogenous effect implies that even a small intervention may generate larger aggregate impacts on society through the spatial/social ''multiplier''. Most studies in the literature on spatial econometrics and peer effects models assume that endogenous effects are linearly proportional to the other's outcome, with a few exceptions (e.g., Jenish, 2016;Xu and Lee, 2015). The linearity of the endogenous effect means that when an individual i is affected by j, the impact of the outcome of j, say y j , on i's outcome y i is equal to c i,j y j for some constant c i,j that is independent of y j . That is, irrespective of the magnitude of y j , the impact of a one-point increase in y j on y i is always equal to c i,j . Based on such a presumption, researchers frequently employ the so-called linear spatial autoregressive (SAR) model:
div.formula: y n,i = ρ 0 n ∑ j=1 w i,j y n,j + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i , i = 1, . . . , n, (1.1)
div.p: where w i,j is a known interaction weight between i and j, x n,i is a vector of explanatory variables, and ε n,i is a zero-mean error term. β 0 is an unknown parameter vector, and the endogenous interaction effect is captured by the parameter ρ 0 (i.e., c i,j = ρ 0 w i,j ). There are vast theoretical and empirical studies that have attempted to account for the endogenous effect by applying models of this type. In the literature on peer effects models, using a model like (1.1) is often justified as a consequence of complementary social interactions, with one's own marginal payoff increasing proportionally to peers' average outcome (cf., Fortin and Boucher, 2016). However, such an assumption is merely made to simplify the analysis and has no theoretical foundation in most cases. For example, consider estimating the spatial spillover effects of regional economic outcomes, such as wages and economic growth. Based on a linear model specification, as in (1.1), many empirical studies have provided evidence of significant spatial endogenous effects of economic growth (e.g., Ertur and Koch, 2007;Fischer, 2011;Sanso-Navarro et al., 2017). However, it would be worth reexamining the results within a framework that allows nonlinear spatial interactions. For example, let the outcome of interest be regional average income, and consider three regions i, j, and k. Suppose that the current income levels of regions j and k are $10,000 and $100,000, respectively, and imagine that we can increase their income levels by $5000 using some economic policy instruments. Then, although both regions achieve the same $5000 improvements, the policy would induce a drastic economic change in region j, whereas it would have only moderate impacts for region k. Hence, in terms of the spatial spillover effects of the policy toward region i, the impact from region j would be larger than that from region k, implying the nonlinearity of the endogenous effects. To account for such nonlinearity, one may suggest replacing y n,j on the right-hand side of (1.1) with ln(y n,j ) or √ y n,j , for instance. However, these model specifications are arbitrary, and if they are incorrect, the resulting parameter estimators are not consistent.
To account for the potential nonlinearity of the endogenous effect, in this paper, we extend model (1.1) to the following nonlinear SAR model:
div.formula: y n,i = n ∑ j=1 w i,j h 0 (y n,j ) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i , i = 1, . . . , n,
div.p: where h 0 is an unknown nonparametric function. The linear SAR model (1.1) is just a special case of this model with h 0 (y n,j ) = ρ 0 y n,j . 1 A major complication in estimating this model is that h 0 is a nonparametric function of the endogenous variable y n,j . The endogeneity of y n,j may be controlled by using j's covariates x n,j as the instrumental variables (IVs). Then, our model can be viewed as a type of nonparametric IV regression model. 2 As a special case, if individual i interacts with only one individual i ′ , the above model is reduced to a partially linear model y n,i = h 0 (y n,i ′ ) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i . The estimation of the partially linear IV model has already been investigated in the literature (see, e.g., Example 2.1, Ai and Chen, 2003; Section 2.4, Chen, 2007;Florens et al., 2012). However, when each individual may interact with more than one person in general, their estimation methods are not directly applicable, and we thus need to develop a new approach.

To estimate our model, following seminal works such as Ai and Chen (2003), Newey and Powell (2003), Blundell et al. (2007), and Chen and Christensen (2018), we approximate the function h 0 in a finite-dimensional sieve space so that the model can be approximated by a simple linear regression model with multiple lagged endogenous variables. In addition, we can treat ∑ n j=1 w i,j h 0 (y n,j ) as a ''single'' endogenous component rather than dealing with the endogeneity of each h 0 (y n,j ) separately, as in the two-stage least squares (2SLS) procedure of Kelejian and Prucha (1998) for estimating the linear SAR model (1.1). Then, combining these ideas, we can develop computationally easy-to-implement 2SLS estimators for h 0 and β 0 . Under some regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimators for both h 0 and β 0 . Furthermore, we provide a nonparametric specification test for the linearity of the endogenous effect.

The test proposed is based on a Wald-type test statistic and is easy to compute. We prove that with appropriate centering and scaling, the test statistic is asymptotically distributed as standard normal under the null hypothesis that h 0 is a linear function (i.e., (1.1) is a true model). To assess the finite sample performance of the proposed sieve estimator and test statistic, we conduct a set of Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that our estimator performs well in finite samples and that our test has approximately the correct size and good power properties as the sample size increases.

As an empirical illustration, we analyze a popular dataset in the literature. Namely, we investigate the determinants of regional development using the dataset created by Gennaioli et al. (2013) (GLLS hereinafter), which comprises 1569 subnational regions from 110 countries. GLLS' data were further examined by Sanso-Navarro et al. (2017) to detect the spatial spillovers of regional productivity (measured in income per capita). Similarly to Sanso-Navarro et al. (2017), we investigate the same data to estimate the form of the endogenous spatial spillovers of productivity. The results show that the endogenous spillover effect is highly nonlinear and concave -decreasing marginal returns to the productivity of surrounding regions. Indeed, the value of the test statistic is sufficiently large to reject the null hypothesis of linearity at any reasonable significance level.

Organization of the paper. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we first formally introduce the model studied in this paper. Since our model is characterized as a system of nonlinear equations, we discuss the conditions under which the model is well defined with a unique solution. After that, for model estimation, we propose our sieve IV estimator. The asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator are investigated in Section 3. In this section, 1 In addition to this paper, several other papers cast doubt on the parametric linear specification of the endogenous interaction effect, such as Malikov and Sun (2017) and Masten (2017). Their approaches are different in spirit from our modeling approach in that while adopting the linearity assumption, they allow for the interaction parameter ρ 0 to be nonparametrically heterogeneous among individuals.

2 For recent surveys of nonparametric IV models, see Newey (2013), Chen and Qiu (2016), and Centorrino et al. (2017).we also propose a test statistic for testing the null hypothesis that h 0 is linear and study its asymptotic distribution. In Section 4, we present the set of Monte Carlo experiments to evaluate the finite sample performance of the proposed estimator and test. Section 5 presents our empirical analysis and Section 6 concludes. All the technical details are relegated to the appendices.

div.head: A nonlinear autoregressive model
div.p: Suppose that we have the data {(y n,i , x n,i ) : 1 ≤ i ≤ n}, where n is the number of observations. As mentioned in the introduction, we modify the standard linear SAR model (1.1) in the following manner:
div.formula: y n,i = n ∑ j=1 w i,j h 0 (y n,j ) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i , i = 1, . . . , n, (2.1)
div.p: where y n,i ∈ R y is the outcome variable of interest, x n,i = (x (1) n,i , . . . , x (dx) n,i ) ⊤ ∈ R x is a d x ×1 vector of exogenous explanatory variables, and w i,j is the (i, j)th element of an n × n prespecified spatial/social interaction matrix W n . 3 The value of each element w i,j of the interaction matrix is determined based on the ''proximity'' between i and j measured in some space, say D. For the location of each unit in this space, we assume the following.

Assumption 2.1 (Sampling Space). Individual units {1, . . . , n} are located in a region D n ⊂ D ⊂ R d , where the cardinality of D n satisfies lim n→∞ |D n | = ∞. The Euclidean distance between any two observations i and j in D, which we denote ∆(i, j), is at least (without loss of generality) 1.

In this assumption, D n denotes the set of possible locations of the sampled units. For spatial data applications, the sampling space D is typically defined by a geographical space with d = 2. For the case of nonspatial data, it is possible to view the space D as a space of general socioeconomic characteristics. Here, we assume that each individual i does not necessarily directly interact with all other n -1 units, but may have a specific reference group based on the distance to them in D. More specifically, let N n,i (δ) be the δ-neighborhood of i:

N n,i (δ) ≡ {j ∈ {1, . . . , n}\{i} : ∆(i, j) ≤ δ}, and we assume the following. Assumption 2.2 (Interaction Matrix). (i) For all i = 1, . . . , n and n ≥ 1, there exists a fixed threshold distance ∆ such that w i,j = 0 for any j ̸ ∈ N n,i ( ∆). (ii) For all n ≥ 1, the row and column sums of the interaction matrix W n are uniformly bounded in absolute value.

From the definition of N n,i (δ), Assumption 2.2(i) also introduces a normalization that the diagonal elements of W n are zero. The existence of the threshold distance ∆ does not necessarily imply a homophily on some particular characteristics -a tendency to interact with similar others -since the definition of D can be freely modified depending on the context of the interaction and it does not need to be explicitly specified in practice. Assumption 2.2(ii) is standard in the literature.
In many empirical studies, the interaction matrix W n is row-normalized so that ∥W n ∥ ∞ = 1, which also implies that ∥W n ∥ 1 is uniformly bounded from Assumption 2.1.

Note that the outcomes y n,i 's are simultaneously endogenously determined following model (2.1), and thus the set of observed outcomes {y n,1 , . . . , y n,n } is an ''equilibrium'' of the system of nonlinear simultaneous equations. In general, the model may not be well defined when the system does not have a model-consistent unique solution. The following assumption guarantees the existence of a unique solution.

div.p: Throughout the rest of the paper, the basic model assumptions given in Assumptions 2.1-2.3 are implicitly maintained.

Then, we can approximate it in a finite-dimensional sieve space (e.g., power series, splines, Fourier series, wavelets). div.p: Remark 2.2 (Identification). One notable feature of our model is that the identifiability of h 0 depends on the magnitude of the structural parameter β 0 . 6 That is, if it were the case that β 0 = 0, z n,i cannot be used as the instruments for y n,i , and h 0 would not be identified. For identification of our model, we need the so-called completeness condition (more precisely, L 2 -completeness, as we have assumed that h 0 is square integrable). According to Proposition 1 of Andrews (2017), this condition is equivalent to the condition that every non-constant function of the endogenous regressor is correlated with some function of the instruments. Hence, if β 0 = 0 and {x n,i } are independent of {ε n,i }, then {y n,i } and {z n,i } are independent by construction, and the completeness condition does not hold.

For a concrete example, consider a simple pair-wise interaction model: y n,i = h 0 (y n,i ′ ) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i , where i ′ denotes i's interacting partner. We assume that (x n,i , x n,i ′ ) are independent of (ε

div.p: Then, the completeness condition in this context can be written as follows: E[h(y n,i ′ ) | x n,i , z n,i ′ ] = 0 almost surely (a.s.) ⇒ h(y n,i ′ ) = 0 a.s. for all square-integrable h (cf., Florens et al., 2012). Then, if β 0 = 0, since the value of

The reciprocal of √ ν JK , which we denote by τ JK ≡ 1/ √ ν JK , can be interpreted as a sieve measure of ill-posedness for our model. Our findings from Table 4.1 are as follows. In DGP 1, where the function h 0 is highly nonlinear, we can significantly reduce the ISB value by increasing J, as expected in theory. In particular, the estimator with J = 1 is clearly insufficiently flexible to capture the shape of h 0 . However, increasing J too quickly deteriorates the estimation performance. For example, when the sample size is 2000, using J = 4 is too flexible, and this results in an IMSE that is twice as large as the cases with J = 3. These results highlight the bias-variance trade-off of our estimator with respect to J. On the other hand, when h 0 can be well approximated (or exactly represented) by a linear function, as in DGPs 2 and 3, using a parsimonious number of J always outperforms the cases with larger J in terms of IMSE. In addition, for DGP 2, although the function h 0 is not very smooth as compared to the other DGPs, it seems that our estimator works satisfactorily, probably because its nonsmoothness is not severe. The choice of K has relatively minor impacts on the performance of the estimator in all DGPs. As shown above, the choice of J is an important factor that governs the performance of the sieve estimator. However, choosing an optimal J is not a simple task, and we leave this issue for future investigation.

The results of estimating (β 01 , β 02 ) are presented in Table 4.2. They show that our estimator performs quite well. The bias and RMSE (root mean squared error) are satisfactorily small, and the coverage rate of the 95% confidence interval is close to the nominal level in all set-ups.

div.head: Test for the linearity of h 0
div.p: We next examine the finite sample performance of the proposed test. The DGPs considered are the same as above; that is, the null hypothesis is true in DGP 3, but not in DGPs 1 and 2. Table 4.3 reports the simulation results for the rejection frequency over 1000 Monte Carlo repetitions at the 10%, 5%, and 1% significance levels.

Our findings from Table 4.3 are as follows. When the function h 0 is highly nonlinear, as in DGP 1, our test has a good power property for all choices of ( J, K ) and all sample sizes. On the contrary, if h 0 becomes closer to a linear function, as in DGP 2, the power of the test decreases, although it can be improved by increasing the sample size. For DGP 2, the choice of J has a certain influence on the performance of our test. Specifically, if too many basis terms are used to approximate h 0 , the increase in the estimation variance diminishes the power of the test considerably. The results for DGP 3 indicate that the size of our test is reasonably well controlled.

div.head: An empirical application: Spatial spillovers of regional productivity
div.p: As mentioned in the introduction, the dataset investigated in this empirical analysis is the one used by GLLS. The authors proposed a new regional development model based on the Lucas model of endogenous growth and presented empirical evidence that regional education level (as a proxy of human capital) is a critical determinant of regional development. In addition, as mentioned by Ertur and Koch (2007), it is commonly observed that national and regional economic growth depends not only on a country's domestic investment in physical and human capital, but also critically on the growth rates and income levels of neighboring regions. Then, Sanso-Navarro et al. (2017) consider a spatial extension of GLLS and provide evidence of the need to account for the presence of spatial dependence to study the determinants of regional productivity. 10 For the estimation, these studies derive a reduced-form model that can be expressed as a standard linear SAR model as in (1.1).

The GLLS data consist of 1569 subnational regions from 110 countries. In this empirical illustration, the outcome variable of interest is regional productivity, measured by income per capita. The explanatory variables considered include, for example, each region's average temperature, oil production, years of education, and the number of ethnic groups inhabited in the region. County-specific dummies are also included. For the definitions of these variables and their detailed summary statistics, see GLLS. After discarding observations with missing data, the analysis is performed on a sample of size 1463.
The model estimated is as follows:
div.formula: ln(Income pc n,i ) = n ∑ j=1 w i,j h 0 (ln(Income pc n,j )) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i , i = 1, . . . , 1463,
div.p: where w i,j is the row-normalized spatial weight between region i and region j created based on the Rook contiguity. For the instruments z n,i , we use all elements of x n,i excluding the country dummies. Note that z n,i includes both continuous and discontinuous variables, say, z c n,i and z d n,i , respectively. 11 Therefore, we use z d n,i without any transformation, and (with an abuse of notation) we redefine q(z n,i ) = (q(z c n,i ) ⊤ , z d⊤ n,i ) ⊤ . We estimate the above model in two alternative ways: using the 2SLS procedure by Kelejian and Prucha (1998) assuming that h 0 (y) = c 0 + ρ 0 y and using the sieve IV method. We use the cubic B-spline basis function with the number of internal knots being 2 for both p and q. The estimation results for the spatial spillover of regional productivity are presented in Fig. 5.1, and Table 5.1 shows the results for β 0 .

Fig. 5.1 shows that the spatial spillover effect is nonlinear and concave. The value of the standardized test statistic is 13.5565, and thus the null hypothesis of linearity is clearly rejected at any reasonable significance level. The result implies that if the economic performances of neighboring regions are high, a one percent increase in them results in less than 10 The GLLS data used in this analysis and spatial information on each region were obtained from the Journal of Applied Econometrics Data Archive: Sanso-Navarro, Vera-Cabello and Ximénez-de-Embún (2017) Human capital spillovers and regional development, Journal of Applied Econometrics, 32, 923-930. 11 Specifically, we set z c n,i = {Temperature, Inverse distance to coast, ln(Population)} and z d n,i = {ln(Oil production per capita), Years of education, ln(No. ethnic groups)}. a one percent increase in own productivity. 12 As reported in Table 5.1, the magnitude and significance of the coefficient estimates are somewhat different between the linear SAR model and the nonlinear model. Then, considering the fact that the linear SAR model is rejected by our specification test, we may conclude that the parameter estimates obtained by the sieve IV method are more reliable.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we consider the sieve IV estimation of cross-sectional interaction models with nonparametric endogenous effects. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator. We also propose a nonparametric specification test for testing the null hypothesis that the endogenous effect is linear in the other's outcome and derive its asymptotic distribution. An empirical illustration using GLLS data indicates the usefulness of the proposed model and test.

There remain some issues not addressed in this study, some of which have been mentioned above. These include choosing an optimal order of the basis expansion J (and K ), accounting for endogenous sample selection, investigating whether the proposed sieve IV estimator can attain the optimal convergence rate, and investigating the sieve IV estimation with shape restrictions (e.g., monotonicity and/or contractivity) on h 0 . In addition, considering a bootstrap version of our test would be important to improve the finite sample properties of the test. Moreover, as suggested by a number of authors (e.g., Goldsmith-Pinkham and Imbens, 2013;Qu and Lee, 2015;Hsieh and Lee, 2016), treating the interaction matrix W n as exogenous and given would be too restrictive in some empirical situations. Lastly, it would be interesting to consider other types of nonparametric endogenous effects models such as y n,i = h 0 ( ∑ n j=1 w i,j y n,j ) + x ⊤ n,i β 0 + ε n,i . We leave these topics to future research.

Since this violates the contraction property required in Assumption 2.3, careful interpretation is needed for such low-productivity regions. To circumvent this issue, it would be important to develop a shape-restricted estimator that imposes |∂h 0 (ỹ)/∂y| < 1 for all ỹ.
